q: A company wants to allow an EC2 instance to access an S3 bucket without storing credentials on the instance. What is the BEST approach?

opts.a: Store access keys in environment variables on the EC2 instance
opts.b: Attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance with appropriate S3 permissions
opts.c: Create an IAM user and hardcode credentials in the application
opts.d: Use the root account credentials on the instance

exp.a: Incorrect. Storing access keys on the instance is a security risk and not a best practice.
exp.b: Correct. Attaching an IAM role to an EC2 instance via an instance profile provides temporary credentials that are automatically rotated, eliminating the need to store static credentials.
exp.c: Incorrect. Hardcoding credentials is a serious security anti-pattern.
exp.d: Incorrect. Using root credentials is never recommended.

q: An IAM user has an Allow policy for s3:* and is also subject to a permissions boundary that only allows s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket. What actions can the user perform?

opts.a: All S3 actions because the identity policy allows s3:*
opts.b: Only s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket
opts.c: No S3 actions because boundaries override everything

exp.a: Incorrect. The permissions boundary limits the effective permissions regardless of the identity policy.
exp.b: Correct. The effective permissions are the intersection of the identity-based policy and the permissions boundary. Only actions allowed in BOTH are permitted.
exp.c: Incorrect. The boundary allows specific actions, and the identity policy also allows them, so the intersection is not empty.
exp.d: Incorrect. s3:PutObject is not in the permissions boundary.

q: A developer needs to allow a Lambda function in Account A to access a DynamoDB table in Account B. What is the correct approach?

opts.a: Create an IAM user in Account B and store credentials in Lambda
opts.b: Create a role in Account B with DynamoDB permissions and a trust policy allowing Account A's Lambda role to assume it
opts.c: Use the root credentials of Account B in the Lambda function
opts.d: Create an IAM group in Account B and add the Lambda function to it

exp.a: Incorrect. Storing cross-account credentials in Lambda is not a best practice.
exp.b: Correct. Cross-account access is achieved by creating a role in the target account (B) with appropriate permissions and a trust policy that allows the source account (A) to assume it.
exp.c: Incorrect. Root credentials should never be used in applications.
exp.d: Incorrect. Lambda functions cannot be added to IAM groups; only users can be group members.

q: An organization requires that all IAM users must use MFA when calling AWS APIs. Which policy condition should be used?

opts.a: aws:SecureTransport
opts.b: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent
opts.c: aws:PrincipalTag

exp.a: Incorrect. aws:SecureTransport checks for HTTPS, not MFA.
exp.b: Correct. The condition key aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent checks whether the request was authenticated with MFA. You can deny actions when this is false.
exp.c: Incorrect. aws:PrincipalTag is used for ABAC, not MFA enforcement.
exp.d: Incorrect. aws:SourceVpc restricts by VPC, not MFA.

q: A policy has the following statement: {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:*", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::mybucket/*"}. What does this allow?

opts.a: All S3 actions on the mybucket bucket itself and all objects inside it
opts.b: All S3 actions only on objects inside mybucket, not on the bucket itself
opts.c: Only read actions on mybucket objects
opts.d: All S3 actions on all buckets in the account

exp.a: Incorrect. The resource ARN 'arn:aws:s3:::mybucket/*' only covers objects inside the bucket, not the bucket itself.
exp.b: Correct. The /* at the end means only objects within the bucket. To include bucket-level actions (like ListBucket), you would also need 'arn:aws:s3:::mybucket' as a separate resource.
exp.c: Incorrect. s3:* includes all actions, not just read.
exp.d: Incorrect. The resource is scoped specifically to mybucket objects.

q: What is the effective permission when an IAM user has no explicit Allow and no explicit Deny for an action?

opts.a: The action is allowed by default
opts.b: The action is implicitly denied
opts.c: The action triggers an MFA prompt
opts.d: The action is allowed for read operations only

exp.a: Incorrect. AWS defaults to deny, not allow.
exp.b: Correct. In the absence of an explicit Allow, all actions are implicitly denied. This is the default deny principle in AWS IAM.
exp.c: Incorrect. No MFA prompt is triggered; the action is simply denied.
exp.d: Incorrect. There is no special treatment for read operations.

q: A company uses AWS Organizations with SCPs. An SCP denies ec2:TerminateInstances, but an IAM policy in a member account explicitly allows it. What happens when a user tries to terminate an instance?

opts.a: The action is allowed because IAM policy overrides SCP
opts.b: The action is denied because SCP restricts the maximum available permissions
opts.c: The action is allowed only if MFA is used
opts.d: The action depends on which policy was created first

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM policies cannot override SCPs.
exp.b: Correct. SCPs set the maximum permissions for member accounts. Even if an IAM policy allows an action, if the SCP denies it, the action is denied. SCPs act as guardrails.
exp.c: Incorrect. MFA does not override SCP restrictions.
exp.d: Incorrect. Policy creation order has no impact on evaluation.

q: Which of the following is the correct order of IAM policy evaluation?

opts.a: Explicit Deny → Organizations SCPs → Resource-based policies → Identity-based policies → Permissions boundaries → Session policies
opts.b: Identity-based policies → SCPs → Resource-based policies → Explicit Deny
opts.c: SCPs → Identity-based policies → Explicit Deny → Permissions boundaries
opts.d: Resource-based policies → Identity-based policies → SCPs → Explicit Deny

exp.a: Correct. AWS evaluates policies in this order: first checking for explicit Deny across all policies, then evaluating SCPs, resource-based policies, identity-based policies, permissions boundaries, and session policies.
exp.b: Incorrect. Explicit Deny is checked first, not last.
exp.c: Incorrect. This order is not accurate.
exp.d: Incorrect. SCPs are evaluated before identity-based policies, not after.

q: A user is part of two IAM groups. Group A allows s3:GetObject. Group B denies s3:GetObject. What is the effective permission?

opts.a: Allowed because Group A allows it
opts.b: Denied because explicit Deny overrides Allow
opts.c: Depends on which group was created first
opts.d: The user gets prompted to choose which group policy applies

exp.a: Incorrect. An Allow cannot override an explicit Deny.
exp.b: Correct. When there is a conflict between an explicit Deny and an explicit Allow, the Deny always wins. This is fundamental to IAM policy evaluation.
exp.c: Incorrect. Creation order does not affect policy evaluation.
exp.d: Incorrect. IAM does not prompt users to choose policies.

q: Which condition key would you use to restrict IAM actions to only allow requests made through a specific VPC endpoint?

opts.a: aws:SourceIp
opts.b: aws:SourceVpce
opts.c: aws:RequestedRegion

exp.a: Incorrect. aws:SourceIp restricts by IP address, not VPC endpoint.
exp.b: Correct. aws:SourceVpce restricts access to requests made through a specific VPC endpoint, useful for ensuring private network access only.
exp.c: Incorrect. aws:RequestedRegion restricts by AWS region.
exp.d: Incorrect. aws:PrincipalOrgID restricts by organization ID.

q: A security team wants to ensure that no IAM user in any member account can create IAM access keys for the root user. Which service should they use?

opts.a: IAM Permissions Boundary
opts.b: AWS Config
opts.c: AWS Organizations Service Control Policy (SCP)

exp.a: Incorrect. Permissions boundaries apply to individual IAM entities, not org-wide root restrictions.
exp.b: Incorrect. AWS Config monitors compliance but doesn't prevent actions.
exp.c: Correct. SCPs can be used to restrict actions across all member accounts in an organization, including preventing access key creation for root users.
exp.d: Incorrect. CloudTrail logs events but doesn't prevent them.

q: What happens when you attach a new permissions boundary to an IAM user who already has identity-based policies?

opts.a: The identity-based policies are automatically deleted
opts.b: The effective permissions become the intersection of the identity policy and the permissions boundary
opts.c: The permissions boundary replaces the identity-based policies
opts.d: The identity-based policies override the permissions boundary

exp.a: Incorrect. Identity-based policies remain intact.
exp.b: Correct. The effective permissions are the intersection (overlap) of the identity-based policy AND the permissions boundary. An action must be allowed in BOTH to be effective.
exp.c: Incorrect. Boundaries do not replace identity policies; they limit them.
exp.d: Incorrect. Identity policies cannot override permissions boundaries.

q: A company needs to grant temporary access to a third-party auditor without creating an IAM user. What is the best approach?

opts.a: Share the root account credentials temporarily
opts.b: Create a cross-account IAM role that the auditor's AWS account can assume
opts.c: Create an IAM user and delete it after the audit
opts.d: Provide VPN access to the company's internal network

exp.a: Incorrect. Never share root credentials.
exp.b: Correct. Creating a cross-account role with appropriate read-only permissions and a trust policy that allows the auditor's account to assume it is the most secure and manageable approach.
exp.c: Incorrect. While possible, managing temporary IAM users is less secure and harder to manage than roles.
exp.d: Incorrect. VPN access doesn't solve the AWS permissions problem.

q: Which API action should be restricted to prevent IAM privilege escalation where a user could attach the AdministratorAccess policy to themselves?

opts.a: iam:CreateUser
opts.b: iam:AttachUserPolicy
opts.c: iam:GetUser

exp.a: Incorrect. Creating a user doesn't directly cause privilege escalation.
exp.b: Correct. iam:AttachUserPolicy allows attaching managed policies. If a user has this permission without resource restrictions, they could attach AdministratorAccess to themselves, causing privilege escalation.
exp.c: Incorrect. GetUser is a read-only action.
exp.d: Incorrect. ListPolicies is read-only and doesn't allow modification.

q: What is the difference between sts:AssumeRole and sts:GetFederationToken?

opts.a: AssumeRole is for roles; GetFederationToken creates temporary credentials scoped down from the caller's permissions
opts.b: They are identical in functionality
opts.c: GetFederationToken is for assuming roles; AssumeRole is for federation
opts.d: AssumeRole works only within the same account; GetFederationToken works cross-account

exp.a: Correct. AssumeRole assumes an existing IAM role. GetFederationToken creates temporary credentials based on the calling IAM user's permissions, optionally scoped down by an inline policy.
exp.b: Incorrect. They serve different purposes.
exp.c: Incorrect. This is reversed.
exp.d: Incorrect. AssumeRole works cross-account as well.

q: An IAM policy uses the condition 'StringEquals': {'s3:prefix': ['home/${aws:username}/*']}. What does the ${aws:username} variable resolve to?

opts.a: The AWS account ID
opts.b: The friendly name of the IAM user making the request
opts.c: The ARN of the IAM role
opts.d: The IP address of the requester

exp.a: Incorrect. ${aws:username} does not resolve to the account ID.
exp.b: Correct. The policy variable ${aws:username} resolves to the friendly name of the IAM user making the request, enabling dynamic per-user policies.
exp.c: Incorrect. The role ARN would use a different variable.
exp.d: Incorrect. IP is referenced through aws:SourceIp.

q: Which of the following is a valid IAM policy variable that can be used in the Resource element?

opts.a: ${aws:CurrentTime}
opts.b: ${aws:username}
opts.c: ${aws:SecureTransport}

exp.a: Incorrect. aws:CurrentTime is used in Condition elements, not as a policy variable in Resource.
exp.b: Correct. ${aws:username} is a valid policy variable that can be used in the Resource element to create dynamic, user-specific resource paths.
exp.c: Incorrect. aws:SecureTransport is a condition key, not usable as a Resource variable.
exp.d: Incorrect. aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is a condition key only.

q: A company wants to allow IAM users to manage their own MFA devices but nothing else. Which actions should be allowed?

opts.a: iam:* on all resources
opts.b: iam:CreateVirtualMFADevice, iam:EnableMFADevice, iam:DeactivateMFADevice, iam:DeleteVirtualMFADevice, iam:ListMFADevices on their own user resource
opts.c: sts:AssumeRole

exp.a: Incorrect. iam:* grants full IAM access, which is far too broad.
exp.b: Correct. These specific actions allow users to create, enable, deactivate, delete, and list their own MFA devices when scoped to their own user ARN.
exp.c: Incorrect. AssumeRole is for assuming roles, not managing MFA.
exp.d: Incorrect. EC2 permissions are unrelated to MFA management.

q: What is the purpose of the 'aws:PrincipalOrgID' condition key?

opts.a: To restrict access to requests from principals within a specific AWS Organization
opts.b: To check the user's email address
opts.c: To verify the instance type
opts.d: To check the region of the request

exp.a: Correct. aws:PrincipalOrgID restricts access to only principals belonging to a specific AWS Organization, useful in resource-based policies to limit cross-account access.
exp.b: Incorrect. Email addresses are not checked with this key.
exp.c: Incorrect. Instance type is not related to this condition key.
exp.d: Incorrect. Region is checked with aws:RequestedRegion.

q: A developer accidentally deleted an IAM customer managed policy. Can it be recovered?

opts.a: Yes, from the IAM recycle bin within 30 days
opts.b: Yes, if versioning was enabled on the policy
opts.c: No, deleted policies cannot be recovered and must be recreated
opts.d: Yes, by contacting AWS Support within 24 hours

exp.a: Incorrect. IAM does not have a recycle bin.
exp.b: Incorrect. Policy versioning allows rollback between versions but does not protect against policy deletion.
exp.c: Correct. Once an IAM managed policy is deleted, it cannot be recovered. It must be recreated manually.
exp.d: Incorrect. AWS Support cannot recover deleted IAM policies.

q: Which of the following scenarios would require a resource-based policy instead of an identity-based policy?

opts.a: Granting an IAM user access to EC2 in the same account
opts.b: Allowing a principal from another AWS account to access your S3 bucket without assuming a role
opts.c: Restricting IAM users to a specific region
opts.d: Enabling MFA for an IAM user

exp.a: Incorrect. Same-account access can be done with identity-based policies.
exp.b: Correct. Resource-based policies (like S3 bucket policies) can grant cross-account access directly without requiring the external principal to assume a role.
exp.c: Incorrect. Region restrictions use identity-based policies with conditions.
exp.d: Incorrect. MFA is configured through IAM settings, not resource-based policies.

q: What is the 'external ID' used for when configuring cross-account role access?

opts.a: To encrypt the session
opts.b: To prevent the confused deputy problem by verifying the identity of the third party
opts.c: To specify the AWS region

exp.a: Incorrect. External ID does not encrypt sessions.
exp.b: Correct. The external ID is a shared secret between you and the third party. It prevents the 'confused deputy' problem where an attacker could trick a service into accessing your resources.
exp.c: Incorrect. External ID has nothing to do with regions.
exp.d: Incorrect. Session duration is set separately.

q: A company policy requires that all S3 operations must be performed over HTTPS. Which IAM policy condition achieves this?

opts.a: "Condition": {"Bool": {"aws:SecureTransport": "true"}}
opts.b: "Condition": {"Bool": {"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "true"}}
opts.c: "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:RequestedRegion": "us-east-1"}}

exp.a: Correct. Using aws:SecureTransport set to true in a Deny statement (with effect Deny when false) ensures that all requests must use HTTPS/SSL.
exp.b: Incorrect. This checks for MFA, not HTTPS.
exp.c: Incorrect. This restricts by region, not transport protocol.
exp.d: Incorrect. This allows all IP addresses, unrelated to HTTPS.

q: An IAM user has an identity-based policy that allows s3:PutObject. A resource-based policy on the S3 bucket also allows s3:PutObject for the same user. Is there any benefit to having both?

opts.a: No, one of them is redundant
opts.b: Yes, within the same account, either one granting access is sufficient, providing defense in depth
opts.c: The resource-based policy always overrides the identity policy
opts.d: Having both causes a conflict and denies the action

exp.a: Incorrect. Both policies are evaluated, and within the same account, either one providing Allow is sufficient.
exp.b: Correct. Within the same AWS account, if either the identity-based policy OR the resource-based policy allows the action, the action is permitted (union of permissions). This provides defense in depth.
exp.c: Incorrect. Neither overrides the other in same-account scenarios; they are additive.
exp.d: Incorrect. Two Allows do not conflict; they are additive.

q: What is the 'confused deputy' problem in IAM?

opts.a: When a user forgets their password
opts.b: When a less-privileged entity tricks a more-privileged entity into performing actions on its behalf
opts.c: When two IAM policies conflict

exp.a: Incorrect. Password issues are not the confused deputy problem.
exp.b: Correct. The confused deputy problem occurs when a less-privileged entity (attacker) tricks a more-privileged entity (trusted service) into performing unauthorized actions. External IDs and aws:SourceArn conditions mitigate this.
exp.c: Incorrect. Policy conflicts are handled by the Deny-overrides-Allow rule.
exp.d: Incorrect. MFA token expiry is unrelated.

q: A session policy is passed when assuming a role using the --policy parameter in sts:AssumeRole. What effect does it have?

opts.a: It expands the permissions beyond what the role allows
opts.b: It further restricts the permissions to the intersection of the role's policies and the session policy
opts.c: It replaces the role's permissions entirely

exp.a: Incorrect. Session policies cannot expand permissions beyond the role's policies.
exp.b: Correct. Session policies act as a filter. The effective permissions are the intersection of the role's identity-based policies and the session policy. It can only further restrict, never expand.
exp.c: Incorrect. Session policies do not replace the role's policies.
exp.d: Incorrect. Session policies do have an effect.

q: What is the maximum number of IAM policies (managed + inline combined) that effectively apply to a single IAM user through direct attachment and group membership?

opts.a: 10 managed policies only
opts.b: 10 direct managed + (10 managed × 10 groups) + inline policies on user and groups
opts.c: 20 policies total

exp.a: Incorrect. This only accounts for directly attached managed policies.
exp.b: Correct. A user can have 10 directly attached managed policies + up to 10 managed policies from each of 10 groups (100) + inline policies on the user and groups. The total effective policies are cumulative.
exp.c: Incorrect. 20 is not the total limit.
exp.d: Incorrect. There are specific limits on each component.

q: A company wants to implement a policy that denies all actions EXCEPT those in the IAM and S3 services. Which policy element combination should they use?

opts.a: Effect: Allow, Action: ["iam:*", "s3:*"]
opts.b: Effect: Deny, NotAction: ["iam:*", "s3:*"], Resource: "*"
opts.c: Effect: Deny, Action: "*", Resource: "*"

exp.a: Incorrect. This only allows IAM and S3 but doesn't deny everything else explicitly.
exp.b: Correct. Using Effect: Deny with NotAction denies everything EXCEPT the listed actions (IAM and S3). This explicitly blocks all other services.
exp.c: Incorrect. This denies all actions including IAM and S3.
exp.d: Incorrect. This would allow everything EXCEPT IAM and S3, which is the opposite of what's needed.

q: Which IAM feature should you use to delegate permission management to developers while preventing them from escalating their own privileges?

opts.a: IAM Groups
opts.b: Permissions Boundaries
opts.c: Resource-based policies

exp.a: Incorrect. Groups organize users but don't prevent privilege escalation.
exp.b: Correct. Permissions boundaries allow administrators to define the maximum permissions that developers can grant when creating roles or users, preventing privilege escalation.
exp.c: Incorrect. Resource-based policies don't address privilege escalation prevention.
exp.d: Incorrect. AWS Config detects compliance issues but doesn't prevent them in real-time.

q: An application uses sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity to authenticate users from Google. What must the IAM role's trust policy include?

opts.a: A Principal specifying the AWS account number
opts.b: A Principal specifying the Google OIDC provider ARN and a Condition checking the token's audience
opts.c: A Principal specifying the root user

exp.a: Incorrect. The principal should be the OIDC provider, not an AWS account.
exp.b: Correct. The trust policy must specify the OIDC identity provider ARN as the Principal and typically includes a Condition to verify the aud (audience) or sub (subject) claim in the token.
exp.c: Incorrect. The root user is not the principal for web identity federation.
exp.d: Incorrect. A trust policy is always required for role assumption.

q: What is the purpose of the 'aws:TagKeys' condition key?

opts.a: To check the value of a specific tag
opts.b: To control which tag keys can be used in a request (e.g., when creating resources)
opts.c: To list all tags in the account

exp.a: Incorrect. Tag values are checked with aws:RequestTag or resource tag conditions.
exp.b: Correct. aws:TagKeys controls which tag keys are allowed or required in a request. This is useful for enforcing tagging standards.
exp.c: Incorrect. aws:TagKeys doesn't list tags.
exp.d: Incorrect. aws:TagKeys doesn't delete tags.

q: How does AWS evaluate policies when a resource-based policy grants access to a principal in a DIFFERENT account?

opts.a: Only the resource-based policy is evaluated
opts.b: Both the resource-based policy in the resource account AND the identity-based policy in the principal's account must allow the action
opts.c: Only the identity-based policy is evaluated
opts.d: Neither is evaluated; cross-account access is always denied

exp.a: Incorrect. Cross-account access requires both sides to grant permission.
exp.b: Correct. For cross-account access (without role assumption), BOTH the resource-based policy in the resource's account AND the identity-based policy in the principal's account must allow the action.
exp.c: Incorrect. The resource-based policy is also evaluated.
exp.d: Incorrect. Cross-account access is possible with proper policies.

q: A company wants to enforce that all newly created IAM users must have a specific tag 'Department'. Which approach should they use?

opts.a: Use AWS Config to detect and report non-compliant users
opts.b: Use an SCP or IAM policy with Condition 'aws:RequestTag/Department' and 'aws:TagKeys' to require the tag during user creation
opts.c: Manually check each user after creation

exp.a: Incorrect. AWS Config detects issues after the fact but doesn't prevent creation without tags.
exp.b: Correct. Using a policy condition with aws:RequestTag/Department and ForAllValues:StringEquals on aws:TagKeys ensures that the Department tag must be provided during user creation.
exp.c: Incorrect. Manual checks are not scalable or reliable.
exp.d: Incorrect. CloudWatch alarms don't enforce IAM tagging.

q: What is the significance of the IAM policy version '2012-10-17'?

opts.a: It is an outdated version that should not be used
opts.b: It is the current and recommended version that supports all policy features including policy variables
opts.c: It only supports Allow statements
opts.d: It is only valid for S3 policies

exp.a: Incorrect. 2012-10-17 is the current version.
exp.b: Correct. Version 2012-10-17 is the current IAM policy language version. It supports all features including policy variables (like ${aws:username}). The older version 2008-10-17 does not support variables.
exp.c: Incorrect. It supports both Allow and Deny.
exp.d: Incorrect. It applies to all IAM policies.

q: An administrator wants to allow an IAM user to pass a specific role to an EC2 instance. Which action must be allowed?

opts.a: iam:CreateRole
opts.b: iam:PassRole
opts.c: sts:AssumeRole

exp.a: Incorrect. CreateRole creates a role but doesn't allow passing it to a service.
exp.b: Correct. The iam:PassRole permission is required to pass a role to an AWS service (like EC2). This prevents users from passing roles with more permissions than they should have.
exp.c: Incorrect. AssumeRole is for assuming a role yourself, not passing it to a service.
exp.d: Incorrect. ec2:RunInstances launches instances but doesn't grant permission to pass a role.

q: What is the relationship between iam:PassRole and iam:CreateRole in terms of security?

opts.a: They are identical permissions
opts.b: PassRole controls who can assign a role to a resource, while CreateRole controls who can create roles — both are privilege escalation vectors if not restricted
opts.c: PassRole is more dangerous than CreateRole

exp.a: Incorrect. They are different permissions.
exp.b: Correct. Both are privilege escalation vectors. CreateRole allows creating roles with any permissions, and PassRole allows assigning those roles to services. Both should be carefully restricted.
exp.c: Incorrect. Both are equally important to restrict.
exp.d: Incorrect. CreateRole does not automatically grant PassRole.

q: A policy uses 'ForAllValues:StringEquals' in the Condition. What does the 'ForAllValues' set operator do?

opts.a: It checks if all values in the request match at least one value in the policy condition
opts.b: It checks if any single value matches
opts.c: It checks if no values match

exp.a: Correct. ForAllValues:StringEquals checks that every value in the request's set of values is a member of the condition's set. If the request key is missing or empty, it evaluates to true (use with caution).
exp.b: Incorrect. That describes ForAnyValue.
exp.c: Incorrect. That is not what ForAllValues does.
exp.d: Incorrect. The condition is evaluated.

q: What does the condition operator 'ArnLike' do compared to 'StringLike'?

opts.a: They are identical
opts.b: ArnLike performs case-insensitive matching on ARN fields and supports wildcards in specific ARN segments
opts.c: ArnLike only works with S3 ARNs
opts.d: StringLike supports ARN matching better than ArnLike

exp.a: Incorrect. They are different operators designed for different use cases.
exp.b: Correct. ArnLike is specifically designed for ARN comparison, supporting wildcards (* and ?) in individual ARN fields (account, region, resource). It treats each ARN component separately.
exp.c: Incorrect. ArnLike works with any ARN.
exp.d: Incorrect. ArnLike is the correct operator for ARN pattern matching.

q: What happens to active sessions when an IAM role's permissions policy is updated?

opts.a: Active sessions immediately get the new permissions
opts.b: Active sessions retain the old permissions until they expire; new sessions get updated permissions
opts.c: Active sessions are immediately terminated
opts.d: Nothing happens; roles cannot be updated while sessions are active

exp.a: Correct. IAM policy changes take effect immediately. Active sessions will have their next API call evaluated against the updated policy, as IAM policies are evaluated at request time.
exp.b: Incorrect. Sessions don't cache permissions; policies are evaluated on each request.
exp.c: Incorrect. Sessions are not terminated when policies change.
exp.d: Incorrect. Roles can be updated at any time.

q: An IAM user needs to switch roles in the AWS Console. What is required?

opts.a: The user must have a new set of access keys
opts.b: The user must have permission to call sts:AssumeRole, and the target role must trust the user's account
opts.c: The user must be in the Administrators group
opts.d: The user must have MFA configured

exp.a: Incorrect. Switch Role in the console doesn't require access keys.
exp.b: Correct. To switch roles, the user needs permission to call sts:AssumeRole, and the target role's trust policy must allow the user (or their account) to assume it.
exp.c: Incorrect. Any user with appropriate permissions can switch roles.
exp.d: Incorrect. MFA may be required by the trust policy but is not universally required.

q: Which AWS CLI command is used to get the identity of the current IAM caller?

opts.a: aws iam get-user
opts.b: aws sts get-caller-identity
opts.c: aws iam list-users

exp.a: Incorrect. get-user shows user details but requires specific permissions and doesn't work for roles.
exp.b: Correct. aws sts get-caller-identity returns the account, ARN, and user ID of the IAM identity making the call. It works for users, roles, and federated identities.
exp.c: Incorrect. list-users lists all users in the account.
exp.d: Incorrect. decode-authorization-message decodes error messages.

q: What is the purpose of the 'aws:SourceAccount' condition key?

opts.a: To check the region of the source
opts.b: To verify that the source account making the request matches a specific account ID, preventing confused deputy attacks
opts.c: To check the user's email

exp.a: Incorrect. aws:SourceAccount doesn't check regions.
exp.b: Correct. aws:SourceAccount verifies the account ID of the entity calling the service. It's commonly used in resource-based policies (like S3) to prevent confused deputy attacks from AWS services.
exp.c: Incorrect. Email is not checked with this condition.
exp.d: Incorrect. This has nothing to do with billing.

q: A Lambda function needs to be invoked by S3 event notifications. Where should the permission be configured?

opts.a: In the Lambda function's IAM execution role
opts.b: In the Lambda function's resource-based policy (allowing s3.amazonaws.com to invoke it)
opts.c: In the S3 bucket's IAM role

exp.a: Incorrect. The execution role defines what Lambda can do, not who can invoke it.
exp.b: Correct. Lambda uses resource-based policies to control which services/accounts can invoke it. The policy must allow the S3 service principal (s3.amazonaws.com) to invoke the function.
exp.c: Incorrect. S3 buckets don't have IAM roles.
exp.d: Incorrect. Root account policies are not the right approach.

q: What is the maximum size of the trust policy document for an IAM role?

opts.a: 2,048 characters
opts.b: 4,096 characters
opts.c: 6,144 characters

exp.a: Correct. The trust policy (assume role policy) for an IAM role has a maximum size of 2,048 characters.
exp.b: Incorrect. The limit is not 4,096 characters.
exp.c: Incorrect. 6,144 is the limit for managed policies.
exp.d: Incorrect. 10,240 is the limit for inline policies on roles.

q: An IAM policy allows ec2:StartInstances but only for instances tagged with 'Environment=Development'. Which condition should be used?

opts.a: "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:RequestTag/Environment": "Development"}}
opts.b: "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"ec2:ResourceTag/Environment": "Development"}}
opts.c: "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:PrincipalTag/Environment": "Development"}}

exp.a: Incorrect. aws:RequestTag is used when creating/tagging resources (the tag being applied in the request), not for checking existing resource tags.
exp.b: Correct. ec2:ResourceTag/Environment checks the existing tag on the EC2 resource. This restricts StartInstances to only instances already tagged with Environment=Development.
exp.c: Incorrect. aws:PrincipalTag checks the tag on the IAM principal making the request, not the resource.
exp.d: Incorrect. aws:TagKeys controls which tag keys are in a request, not resource tags.

q: What is the difference between 'aws:RequestTag' and 'ec2:ResourceTag' condition keys?

opts.a: They are identical
opts.b: aws:RequestTag checks tags being applied in the current request; ec2:ResourceTag checks tags already existing on the resource
opts.c: ec2:ResourceTag checks request tags; aws:RequestTag checks existing tags

exp.a: Incorrect. They serve different purposes.
exp.b: Correct. aws:RequestTag checks the tags being sent in the API request (e.g., during resource creation). ec2:ResourceTag checks the tags already present on existing resources.
exp.c: Incorrect. This is reversed.
exp.d: Incorrect. They work with EC2 and other services respectively.

q: A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. They want to prevent any account from leaving the organization. Which approach should they use?

opts.a: Create an IAM policy denying organizations:LeaveOrganization
opts.b: Create an SCP denying organizations:LeaveOrganization and attach it to all OUs
opts.c: Disable the root user in all member accounts
opts.d: Use AWS Config to prevent it

exp.a: Incorrect. An IAM policy only affects specific users, not all principals including root.
exp.b: Correct. An SCP denying organizations:LeaveOrganization applies to all principals in the member accounts (including root in member accounts), preventing any account from leaving.
exp.c: Incorrect. Root users cannot be disabled.
exp.d: Incorrect. AWS Config cannot prevent actions in real-time.

q: What is role chaining in IAM?

opts.a: Creating multiple roles at once
opts.b: When a role assumes another role, creating a chain of role assumptions
opts.c: Attaching multiple policies to a role
opts.d: Adding a role to multiple groups

exp.a: Incorrect. Role chaining is not about creating multiple roles.
exp.b: Correct. Role chaining occurs when a role assumes another role. The session duration is limited to a maximum of 1 hour when role chaining, regardless of the role's maximum session duration setting.
exp.c: Incorrect. Attaching policies is not role chaining.
exp.d: Incorrect. Roles cannot be added to groups.

q: What is the maximum session duration when using role chaining?

opts.a: 15 minutes
opts.b: 1 hour
opts.c: 12 hours

exp.a: Incorrect. 15 minutes is the minimum for AssumeRole, not the limit for chaining.
exp.b: Correct. When role chaining (a role assumes another role), the maximum session duration is limited to 1 hour, regardless of the role's configured maximum session duration.
exp.c: Incorrect. 12 hours is the max for direct role assumption, not role chaining.
exp.d: Incorrect. 36 hours is the max for GetFederationToken.

q: Which service generates temporary credentials that include an Access Key ID starting with 'ASIA'?

opts.a: IAM (long-term credentials)
opts.b: AWS STS (temporary credentials)
opts.c: AWS KMS

exp.a: Incorrect. Long-term IAM credentials start with 'AKIA'.
exp.b: Correct. AWS STS temporary credentials have Access Key IDs starting with 'ASIA', which distinguishes them from permanent credentials that start with 'AKIA'.
exp.c: Incorrect. KMS handles encryption keys, not access credentials.
exp.d: Incorrect. While Cognito uses STS behind the scenes, the service that generates 'ASIA' prefixed keys is STS.

q: A developer wants to restrict access so that IAM users can only launch EC2 instances in the us-east-1 region. Which condition key and policy approach should be used?

opts.a: Use aws:RequestedRegion with StringEquals 'us-east-1' in an Allow policy
opts.b: Use aws:SourceIp to restrict by region
opts.c: Use aws:CurrentTime to restrict by region
opts.d: Create the IAM user only in us-east-1

exp.a: Correct. Using the condition key aws:RequestedRegion with StringEquals 'us-east-1' in a policy restricts the user to making requests only in the us-east-1 region.
exp.b: Incorrect. aws:SourceIp restricts by IP address, not region.
exp.c: Incorrect. aws:CurrentTime restricts by time, not region.
exp.d: Incorrect. IAM is global; users are not created in specific regions.

q: What is the recommended way to provide AWS credentials to an application running on an EC2 instance?

opts.a: Store credentials in the application's configuration file
opts.b: Use environment variables with hardcoded access keys
opts.c: Attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance using an instance profile
opts.d: Store credentials in an S3 bucket and download them at startup

exp.a: Incorrect. Configuration files with credentials are a security risk.
exp.b: Incorrect. Hardcoded environment variables are not best practice.
exp.c: Correct. Using an instance profile with an IAM role provides temporary, automatically rotated credentials to the EC2 instance. The credentials are accessed via the instance metadata service.
exp.d: Incorrect. Storing credentials in S3 adds unnecessary complexity and risk.

q: What is the EC2 instance metadata endpoint URL where IAM role credentials are retrieved?

opts.a: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role-name>
opts.b: http://192.168.1.1/credentials
opts.c: https://iam.amazonaws.com/credentials

exp.a: Correct. EC2 instances retrieve IAM role credentials from the instance metadata service at http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role-name>.
exp.b: Incorrect. This is not the metadata endpoint.
exp.c: Incorrect. IAM credentials are not retrieved from the IAM API endpoint.
exp.d: Incorrect. This is not a valid metadata endpoint.
